messages.content: Predict the actual response of a real participant. Use the stated rules and information available at this stage, without advice, moral judgment or explanation. Money is measured in Tokens; 100 Tokens equal £1. This is the first allocation task in the main study. The fixed participation payment is £1.80, and the participant starts with an additional 75 Tokens. A randomly paired other person faces the same task. There are 24 two-option allocations on one page. Each option states signed changes in your and the other person’s Tokens: positive means gaining that amount and negative means losing it. The computer selects one allocation for payment and randomly chooses whether your decision or the other person’s decision determines the allocation. No choices are revealed to the other person during play. For each of the 24 items choose logical option 1 or 2 as defined below. Actual screen order and left/right positions may be randomized; the requested output uses the fixed item order below. These are separate conditional allocations, not 24 additions to one payoff. Output only a JSON array of 24 integers, each 1 or 2.

Predict the actual response of a real participant. Use the stated rules and information available at this stage, without advice, moral judgment or explanation. Money is measured in Tokens; 100 Tokens equal £1. The main-study point-allocation page is complete. In this next part you see eight avatars representing different real people who played an earlier dictator game. Each earlier allocator had 100 Tokens for their own use plus 100 Tokens they could distribute; their gift could be 0–100 and their total retention 200 minus that gift. Avatars are photographs matched to appearance characteristics, not actual photographs of the allocators. Guess how many Tokens the current allocator actually gave, rather than how much they should give or how much you would give. One guess is randomly selected: being within 5 Tokens of the real gift earns 70 Tokens. The real gift has not yet been shown in this part. Output only a number from 0 to 100.

Predict the actual response of a real participant. Use the stated rules and information available at this stage, without advice, moral judgment or explanation. Money is measured in Tokens; 100 Tokens equal £1. You are now in the main-study attractiveness-rating part, after the allocation page, eight gift guesses and three presentations of each of eight other allocators’ actual gifts with recall questions. For the current photo, two sliders appear together. First rate how attractive you personally find the person, 0 very unattractive to 100 very attractive. Second estimate the attractiveness rating most participants in this study would give, on the same scale. The second is a prediction of the most common rating, not an average and not your first rating repeated. The instructions promise 70 Tokens if this estimate is within 5 points of the most common response; the local materials do not settle payment selection across all such ratings. Neither rating transfers Tokens to the person pictured. Output only a JSON array [personal rating, predicted most-common rating], each number 0–100.

Output only a JSON array of 24 integers, each 1 or 2.

Money is measured in Tokens; 100 Tokens equal £1. This is the first allocation task in the main study. The fixed participation payment is £1.80, and the participant starts with an additional 75 Tokens. A randomly paired other person faces the same task. There are 24 two-option allocations on one page. Each option states signed changes in your and the other person’s Tokens: positive means gaining that amount and negative means losing it. The computer selects one allocation for payment and randomly chooses whether your decision or the other person’s decision determines the allocation. No choices are revealed to the other person during play. For each of the 24 items choose logical option 1 or 2 as defined below. Output only a JSON array of 24 integers, each 1 or 2.

Output only a JSON array of 24 integers, each 1 or 2.

The fixed participation payment is £1.80, and the participant starts with an additional 75 Tokens. A randomly paired other person faces the same task. There are 24 two-option allocations on one page. Each option states signed changes in your and the other person’s Tokens: positive means gaining that amount and negative means losing it. The computer selects one allocation for payment and randomly chooses whether your decision or the other person’s decision determines the allocation. No choices are revealed to the other person during play. For each of the 24 items choose logical option 1 or 2 as defined below. Actual screen order and left/right positions may be randomized; the requested output uses the fixed item order below. These are separate conditional allocations, not 24 additions to one payoff. Output only a JSON array of 24 integers, each 1 or 2.

Actual screen order and left/right positions may be randomized; the requested output uses the fixed item order below. These are separate conditional allocations, not 24 additions to one payoff. Output only a JSON array of 24 integers, each 1 or 2.

No choices are revealed to the other person during play. For each of the 24 items choose logical option 1 or 2 as defined below. Actual screen order and left/right positions may be randomized; the requested output uses the fixed item order below. These are separate conditional allocations, not 24 additions to one payoff. Output only a JSON array of 24 integers, each 1 or 2.

Output only a JSON array of 24 integers, each 1 or 2.

Output only a JSON array of 24 integers, each 1 or 2.

Money is measured in Tokens; 100 Tokens equal £1. This is the first allocation task in the main study. The fixed participation payment is £1.80, and the participant starts with an additional 75 Tokens. A randomly paired other person faces the same task. There are 24 two-option allocations on one page. Each option states signed changes in your and the other person’s Tokens: positive means gaining that amount and negative means losing it. The computer selects one allocation for payment and randomly chooses whether your decision or the other person’s decision determines the allocation. No choices are revealed to the other person during play. For each of the 24 items choose logical option 1 or 2 as defined below. Actual screen order and left/right positions may be randomized; the requested output uses the fixed item order below. These are separate conditional allocations, not 24 additions to one payoff. Output only a JSON array of 24 integers, each 1 or 2.

Money is measured in Tokens; 100 Tokens equal £1. This is the first allocation task in the main study. The fixed participation payment is £1.80, and the participant starts with an additional 75 Tokens. A randomly paired other person faces the same task. There are 24 two-option allocations on one page. Each option states signed changes in your and the other person’s Tokens: positive means gaining that amount and negative means losing it. The computer selects one allocation for payment and randomly chooses whether your decision or the other person’s decision determines the allocation. No choices are revealed to the other person during play. For each of the 24 items choose logical option 1 or 2 as defined below. Output only a JSON array of 24 integers, each 1 or 2.

The fixed participation payment is £1.80, and the participant starts with an additional 75 Tokens. A randomly paired other person faces the same task. There are 24 two-option allocations on one page. The computer selects one allocation for payment and randomly chooses whether your decision or the other person’s decision determines the allocation. No choices are revealed to the other person during play. For each of the 24 items choose logical option 1 or 2 as defined below. Output only a JSON array of 24 integers, each 1 or 2.

Money is measured in Tokens; 100 Tokens equal £1. This is the first allocation task in the main study. The fixed participation payment is £1.80, and the participant starts with an additional 75 Tokens. A randomly paired other person faces the same task. There are 24 two-option allocations on one page. Each option states signed changes in your and the other person’s Tokens: positive means gaining that amount and negative means losing it. The computer selects one allocation for payment and randomly chooses whether your decision or the other person’s decision determines the allocation. Output only a JSON array of 24 integers, each 1 or 2.

Money is measured in Tokens; 100 Tokens equal £1. This is the first allocation task in the main study. The fixed participation payment is £1.80, and the participant starts with an additional 75 Tokens. A randomly paired other person faces the same task. There are 24 two-option allocations on one page. Each option states signed changes in your and the other person’s Tokens: positive means gaining that amount and negative means losing it. The computer selects one allocation for payment and randomly chooses whether your decision or the other person’s decision determines the allocation. No choices are revealed to the other person during play. For each of the 24 items choose logical option 1 or 2 as defined below. Actual screen order and left/right positions may be randomized; the requested output uses the fixed item order below. These are separate conditional allocations, not 24 additions to one payoff. Output only a JSON array of 24 integers, each 1 or 2.
